# Obesity & metabolic syndrome

> *A patient with a "reassuring" BMI can still be carrying the fat that matters. Obesity and the
> metabolic syndrome are a pattern written by biology and environment together, so the clinical task
> is to read the pattern, start lifestyle-first care and know what to refer onward, without stigma.*

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
- Classify an adult's weight status on Singapore's lower BMI and waist cut-offs, and explain why
  Singapore acts earlier than the WHO lines.
- Apply the harmonised any-three-of-five definition of the metabolic syndrome, and explain why it is a
  risk marker and not a single disease.
- Explain how visceral and ectopic fat, adipose inflammation and the adipokine shift produce insulin
  resistance and the metabolic-syndrome cluster.
- Explain why ultra-processed foods and sugar-sweetened drinks drive overeating: what is eaten shapes
  how much is eaten.
- Plan lifestyle-first care across diet, activity, sleep, stress and behaviour change aimed at a
  5–10% loss, and recognise medication and surgery as specialist tiers to refer for.
- Frame a weight conversation in weight-inclusive, person-first language, and explain why weight
  stigma harms health.
:::

## Obesity & metabolic syndrome at a glance {#sec-overview}

Over- and under-nutrition are the two tails of malnutrition, and obesity is the more familiar one
(undernutrition is in the *Undernutrition & Malnutrition* chapter). Obesity is also the entry point to
a cardiometabolic cascade, because the same central, insulin-resistant fat that defines it drives much
of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease (see the *Type 2 Diabetes* and *Cardiovascular Disease &
Hypertension* chapters).

Three ideas shape how over-nutrition is recognised and managed:

- Singapore acts at lower BMI and waist cut-offs than the global ones, for a physiological reason.
- Diet quality is a larger lever than calorie arithmetic alone, and sleep and stress are levers too.
- How a weight conversation is framed, without stigma and with the person first, is part of clinical
  care.

The physiology underneath (how energy balance is measured, and how leptin, ghrelin and the
hypothalamus set appetite) is in the [*Energy Balance*](energy-balance.qmd) and
[*Appetite & Weight Regulation*](appetite-weight-regulation.qmd) chapters.

## Recognising obesity and the metabolic syndrome {#sec-recognising}

### The phenotype: BMI, waist and why Singapore acts earlier {#sec-phenotype}

BMI (weight ÷ height², introduced in the [*Energy Balance*](energy-balance.qmd#sec-measuring)
chapter) is a screening proxy, not a measurement of fat. It cannot separate muscle from fat or say
where the fat sits. That limitation matters in Singapore, because Singaporean adults carry more body
fat, and proportionally more visceral fat, at a given BMI than the Western populations on which the
WHO cut-offs were built.

The local Yishun Study made the gap concrete. Matched for BMI, age and sex, Singaporeans had higher
percentage body fat, and classifying by body fat instead of BMI flagged far more adults as carrying
excess body fat than BMI did [@chen2021yishun]. Because Asians reach diabetes and cardiovascular risk
at a lower BMI, Singapore shifts its action points down from the WHO cut-offs
[@whoExpert2004AsianBMI].

There are therefore two number-lines for BMI:

| Number-line | Lower threshold | Upper threshold |
|---|---|---|
| WHO (global) | Overweight: BMI ≥25 kg/m² | Obese: BMI ≥30 kg/m² |
| Singapore (clinical action) [@hpbmoh2016obesityCPG; @sgObesityBMI] | Intervene: BMI ≥23 kg/m² | High risk: BMI ≥27.5 kg/m² |

The most useful bedside addition is the waist circumference, because it reads central fat, the
metabolically active kind. The Asian cut-offs sit lower here too: ≥90 cm in men and ≥80 cm in women
[@alberti2009harmonizingMetS; @sgObesityBMI]. A waist at or above the cut-off defines **central
obesity**, excess fat carried around the abdomen. BMI and waist are therefore read together, never
BMI alone.

::: {.example}
A patient with a "reassuring" BMI of 24 kg/m² and a waist over the cut-off is still carrying risk.
:::

### The metabolic syndrome: a cluster, not a disease {#sec-mets}

Central fat rarely travels alone. The **metabolic syndrome** is the tendency for five cardiometabolic
problems to appear together. Its harmonised international definition is any three of the following
five, with no single obligatory component [@alberti2009harmonizingMetS]:

- central obesity: waist ≥90 cm (men) or ≥80 cm (women) in Asian populations;
- raised triglycerides: ≥1.7 mmol/L;
- low HDL cholesterol: <1.0 mmol/L (men) or <1.3 mmol/L (women);
- raised blood pressure: ≥130/85 mmHg;
- raised fasting glucose: ≥5.6 mmol/L.

Treatment for a component counts the same as an abnormal reading.

Two linked problems sit at the hub of the cluster: central fat and **insulin resistance**, a
reduced response of the body's cells to insulin. At first, the pancreas compensates by making more
insulin to keep blood glucose normal. The shared hub is why the five components appear together. The syndrome is therefore best read as a risk marker, not a single disease with a single drug: it
flags a markedly raised risk of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease
[@kaurMetsDefinitionsReview2014; @metsDefinitionsControversies2011]. The label is a prompt to look at the whole cluster and its shared
root. Local data add a further nuance: the components do not always behave as one tidy syndrome
across Singapore's ethnic groups [@angMetsSingaporeNHS2005].

In the interactive below, toggle a patient's findings to see when the three-of-five threshold is met,
and how sleep loss and stress feed the same hub.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why does Singapore start intervening at a BMI of 23, when the WHO line calls no one overweight until 25?
BMI cannot show how much of the weight is fat or where it sits. Singaporean adults carry more body
fat, and proportionally more visceral fat, at a given BMI than the Western populations behind the WHO
cut-offs. Asians therefore reach diabetes and cardiovascular risk at a lower BMI, so the WHO cut-offs
would miss real risk. The Yishun Study showed the gap: classifying by body fat flagged far more adults
than BMI did.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a patient has raised blood pressure, low HDL and raised fasting glucose, but a waist under the cut-off. Does she have the metabolic syndrome, and what follows from the label?
Yes. The harmonised definition is any three of five components with no obligatory one, so central
obesity is not required. The label is a risk marker for type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease,
so it prompts a look at the whole cluster and its shared root (insulin resistance at the hub), not
a single drug for "the syndrome".
:::

## The science underneath: why the risks cluster and the weight accumulates {#sec-science}

### How obesity produces the cluster {#sec-mechanism}

The five problems travel together because body fat is an active endocrine organ: where it sits and
how it behaves link a waistline to a blood-glucose reading. (The normal mechanics of fat storage and
insulin action are in the [*Energy Balance*](energy-balance.qmd) and
[*Integrative Metabolism*](integrative-metabolism.qmd#sec-switch) chapters; here we follow how they go
wrong.) Four terms describe the process:

Ectopic fat
: Fat deposited inside organs such as the liver and muscle, instead of under the skin.

Chronic low-grade inflammation
: A persistent, mild inflammatory state; in obesity it is driven by immune cells (macrophages)
  recruited into enlarged, stressed fat tissue.

Adipokines
: The hormones and signalling proteins that fat tissue releases. They include adiponectin, which is
  insulin-sensitising and anti-inflammatory.

Lipotoxicity
: The harm done when free fatty acids and ectopic lipid spill over into non-fat tissues; in liver and
  muscle it disrupts insulin signalling.

![How obesity produces the metabolic syndrome. A chronic energy surplus enlarges visceral and ectopic fat, which becomes inflamed and shifts its adipokine output, driving insulin resistance (the shared hub) and blunting satiety, so the five-component cluster emerges from one mechanism.](/figures/mechanisms/obesity-pathophysiology.svg){#fig-obesity-pathophysiology width="88%" fig-align="center"}

The chain starts with where the fat is stored. A chronic energy surplus enlarges fat cells, but the
harmful growth is in visceral fat, packed around the abdominal organs, and in ectopic fat, not in the
subcutaneous fat under the skin. Visceral fat drains straight to the liver and behaves differently
from subcutaneous fat: it is an independent marker of cardiometabolic risk, over and above BMI
[@neeland2019visceral]. The waist circumference, a bedside read of central fat, therefore adds a great
deal to what BMI shows.

Enlarged fat then becomes inflamed fat. As fat cells enlarge and outgrow their blood supply, the
tissue becomes stressed and recruits macrophages, and it settles into chronic low-grade inflammation.
This adipose inflammation is now understood to cause insulin resistance rather than merely accompany
it [@hotamisligil2006inflammation]. The adipokine profile shifts at the same time: adiponectin falls,
while pro-inflammatory signals such as tumour necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), interleukin-6 (IL-6) and
resistin rise [@ouchi2011adipokines].

The result is insulin resistance, the hub of the cluster. Alongside the inflammation, lipotoxicity
jams insulin signalling in the liver and muscle [@samuel2012mechanisms], and together they make the
body's cells less responsive to insulin. Insulin resistance raises blood glucose, drives the liver to
over-produce triglyceride (raising triglycerides and lowering HDL) and contributes to higher blood
pressure, so the five components emerge from one mechanism.

Fat also signals the brain, and in obesity the signal goes wrong. Leptin, the satiety signal from
fat, runs high, but central leptin signalling is blunted. This leptin resistance (see the
[*Appetite & Weight Regulation*](appetite-weight-regulation.qmd#sec-leptin) chapter) weakens satiety
and makes the surplus harder to reverse [@myers2010leptin]. The same biology that builds the cluster
also defends the weight, which is why lifestyle change is a physiological lever, not a test of
willpower.

### Why weight accumulates: energy balance, but quality is the lever {#sec-accumulation}

At the level of physics, weight gain is a chronic positive energy balance: small daily surpluses
banked over years (see the [*Energy Balance*](energy-balance.qmd) chapter). "Eat less, move more"
is a weak clinical lever on its own, however, because it treats every calorie as equal, and what is
eaten shapes how much gets eaten. Two drivers do most of the work.

**Ultra-processed foods drive overeating even when the nutrients are matched.** The evidence comes
from the controlled inpatient trial met in the *Digestion & Absorption* chapter. People freely eating
an ultra-processed diet took in about 500 kcal a day more than the same people on an unprocessed diet,
and gained weight, although the two diets were matched for sugar, fat, fibre and salt [@hall2019upf].
Higher ultra-processed intake tracks with obesity and, more convincingly, with incident diabetes and
cardiovascular outcomes across large populations [@lane2024upfumbrella].

**Sugar-sweetened drinks add energy the body barely notices.** Liquid sugar is poorly compensated:
people do not eat correspondingly less at the next meal, and higher intake produces dose-dependent
weight gain [@nguyen2023ssb]. Swapping to a "diet" drink is not the fix the label implies. The WHO
advises against relying on **non-sugar sweeteners**, the sugar substitutes in "diet" drinks, for
weight control, so the better swap is water or an unsweetened drink, plus habit change [@who2023nss].

The targets are simple to state: free sugars under 10% of energy (ideally under 5%), saturated fat
under 10%, *trans* fat under 1% and salt under 5 g a day [@who2020diet; @who2015sugars]. Singapore
translates them into tools that need no arithmetic: My Healthy Plate (a quarter wholegrains, a
quarter protein, half fruit and vegetables) and the Nutri-Grade A–D grades on drinks
[@hpbHealthyPlate; @hpbNutriGrade]. The message is patterns over single nutrients, and minimally
processed food over ultra-processed [@aha2021diet].

::: {.callout-note}
## 🔬 Food science: why "same nutrients" can still mean more energy eaten
Soft, energy-dense, quick-to-eat foods are eaten faster and in greater volume before fullness signals
catch up, so intake runs ahead of need even when a diet is matched gram for gram on sugar, fat and
fibre. That is the finding of the inpatient feeding trial, and it makes processing, as well as
composition, a lever worth naming [@hall2019upf].
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🍜 Eating out
The hawker plate is where most of this is decided. Energy-dense staples add up fast: a plate of char
kway teow runs to roughly 744 kcal with about 38 g of fat, close to a whole day's fat in one dish
[@healthhubHawkerSwaps]. Several lower-density swaps still fit My Healthy Plate:

- thunder tea rice;
- non-fried yong tau foo (more vegetables and tofu, clear soup);
- sliced fish bee hoon soup;
- Teochew porridge with lean sides.

For drinks, read the Nutri-Grade: choose grade A or B, or order *kopi-o kosong*, *teh-o kosong* or
plain water instead of a grade C or D condensed-milk or bubble-tea drink.
:::

![Char kway teow, a Singapore hawker favourite and a useful energy-density anchor: roughly 744 kcal and 38 g of fat in one plate.](/figures/food/char-kway-teow.jpg){#fig-char-kway-teow width="70%" fig-align="center"}

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: two men have the same BMI, but one carries much more visceral fat. Why is he more likely to develop the metabolic-syndrome cluster?
Visceral fat drains straight to the liver and is an independent marker of cardiometabolic risk over
and above BMI. Enlarged visceral and ectopic fat becomes inflamed and shifts its adipokine output
(adiponectin falls, pro-inflammatory signals rise), and with lipotoxicity this produces insulin
resistance. Insulin resistance then raises glucose and triglycerides, lowers HDL and contributes to
higher blood pressure.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: the inpatient trial matched its two diets for sugar, fat, fibre and salt. Why did people still eat about 500 kcal a day more on the ultra-processed diet, and what follows for advice?
Because the diets were matched on composition, the difference lies in the form of the food. Soft,
energy-dense, quick-to-eat foods are eaten faster and in greater volume before fullness signals catch
up, though which of these features matters most is still debated. Processing, as well as
composition, is therefore a lever. Advice works at the level of the pattern: minimally processed food
over ultra-processed, and water or an unsweetened drink over a sugar-sweetened one.
:::

## Managing over-nutrition {#sec-managing}

### Lifestyle first, then refer {#sec-lifestyle}

The weight-loss target is modest. A sustained 5–10% weight loss yields a disproportionate,
dose-dependent cardiometabolic payoff, improving glucose, blood pressure and lipids well out of
proportion to the change on the scale [@wing2011modest]. Lifestyle change is the cornerstone of care:
every other treatment is added to it, not substituted for it.

Five levers make up first-line care, and two of them, sleep and stress, are routinely under-used (see
the [*Appetite & Weight Regulation*](appetite-weight-regulation.qmd#sec-sleep-stress) chapter).

**Diet pattern.** The diet lever is a set of pattern-level substitutions built on My Healthy Plate,
not a branded diet, aiming for a 5–10% loss over 6–12 months [@aceBmiControl2026].

**Physical activity.** Activity works partly independently of the scale: it cuts visceral fat,
improves insulin sensitivity and preserves lean mass even when weight barely moves
[@kolnes2021exercisefat]. Diet quality remains the larger lever for weight, so the two are paired.

**Sleep.** Sleep is a modifiable weight lever. Short or poor sleep raises energy intake with no
matching rise in expenditure, and extending sleep brings intake back down [@alkhatib2017;
@tasali2022sleepextension]. Short habitual sleep also tracks with more central obesity
[@kohanmoo2024shortsleep]. The appetite-hormone mechanism is less certain: the classic account, in
which leptin falls and ghrelin rises, is echoed observationally, but a 2025 meta-analysis of trials
found no reliable hormone shift [@spiegel2004; @sleepHormonesMeta2025]. Intake is the reliable
signal; the hormone story suggests a direction, not a proven mechanism.

**Stress.** Chronic stress and cortisol bias eating toward energy-dense comfort food and channel fat
to the abdomen, a self-reinforcing loop that feeds the hub of central fat and insulin resistance
[@dallman2003]. Mindfulness programmes for weight are still exploratory, so the mechanism can be
named but a fix cannot be promised [@daubenmier2011].

**Behaviour change.** Behaviour-change skills make the other four levers stick (see the
[*Behaviour-Change Counselling*](behaviour-change-counselling.qmd) chapter).

::: {.callout-note}
## The treatment ladder, and where recognition stops
Above lifestyle sit two specialist tiers: anti-obesity medication (including the newer GLP-1
receptor agonists) and **metabolic-bariatric surgery** (weight-loss surgery), which can achieve
substantially greater loss for selected patients [@lee2023obesitylandscape]. The task at this stage
is to **recognise that these tiers exist and refer**, not to prescribe or select them.

Two evidence cautions apply to what lifestyle change can be expected to achieve. First, the landmark
trials showing that lifestyle change can prevent or even remit diabetes used intensive, structured
programmes. The Diabetes Prevention Program was a 16-session curriculum [@dpp2002], and DiRECT's ~46% remission
applied to early, non-insulin-treated patients and is untested in Asian primary care
[@lean2018direct]. Second, improving those risk factors is not the same as preventing cardiovascular
events: an intensive lifestyle programme in established diabetes improved markers but did not reduce
cardiovascular events [@lookahead2013]. (The mechanics of remission are in the *Type 2 Diabetes*
chapter.)
:::

### Weight-inclusive care: the framing is part of the treatment {#sec-weight-inclusive}

How a weight conversation is framed changes its outcome, so framing is a clinical skill.
**Weight stigma** is negative attitudes towards, and treatment of, people because of their weight,
such as blame, shaming or disrespect. Weight stigma is a health hazard [@tomiyama2014cobwebs;
@phelan2015impact; @puhl2023barriers]:

- it degrades the quality of care;
- it drives patients to avoid appointments;
- by raising cortisol and comfort-eating, it can paradoxically promote weight gain, the loop captured
  by the Cyclic Obesity/Weight-Based Stigma (COBWEBS) model.

International consensus now condemns weight stigma outright and asks clinicians to switch focus from
the scale to health and behaviour [@rubino2020consensus; @tylka2014weightinclusive;
@batterham2020switchingfocus]. Care built on that shift is **weight-inclusive**: it anchors counselling
on health behaviours and metabolic markers instead of on the scale alone. Weight stigma is a live issue
in Singapore: in a local survey most respondents had felt weight-stigmatised, and a fifth felt
disrespected or discouraged by a healthcare worker [@chue2022stigmasg; @goff2023sgweightbias].

::: {.callout-important}
## The language shift
The framing comes down to three habits [@weghuber2023peoplefirst; @batterham2020switchingfocus]:

- Use **person-first language**, which names the person before the condition ("a person with
  obesity", not "an obese patient").
- Ask permission before discussing weight.
- Set goals around health behaviours and metabolic markers, not the scale alone, while still holding
  the ~5–10% target that earns the metabolic payoff.

Shaming does not motivate; it backfires.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a patient has lost 6% of his weight, but his BMI still puts him in the high-risk band. Why is the loss still worthwhile?
A sustained 5–10% loss gives a disproportionate, dose-dependent cardiometabolic payoff, improving
glucose, blood pressure and lipids well out of proportion to the change on the scale. Physical
activity adds to this, cutting visceral fat and improving insulin sensitivity even when weight barely
moves. The target is metabolic health.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why can shaming a patient about weight make the weight harder to lose?
Weight stigma degrades the quality of care and drives patients to avoid appointments, so they receive
less of the care that helps. Stigma also raises cortisol and comfort-eating, which can promote weight
gain (the COBWEBS loop). Person-first, permission-based framing is therefore part of the treatment.
:::

## The Singapore picture {#sec-singapore}

**Singapore reports obesity at one threshold and acts at another.** Population obesity is reported at
the WHO ≥30 threshold for international comparability, and on that measure it rose from 10.5% to
12.7% between 2019–20 and 2023–24; clinical action starts far earlier, and the ≥27.5 high-risk band
has held steady at roughly 1 in 5 adults [@mohNPHS2024]. "12.7% obese" is the newspaper figure;
≥27.5 and ≥23 are the clinic figures. Over the same window, national physical activity recovered to 84.7%
and obesity still rose, a Singapore-grounded argument for putting diet quality ahead of "just
exercise more" [@mohNPHS2024].

**The components of the cluster are common.** The survey reports the components separately.
Hypertension affects about 1 in 3 adults, raised blood lipids about 1 in 3 and
diabetes roughly 1 in 11: the population denominators behind the clustering idea [@mohNPHS2024].

**Obesity and diabetes follow an ethnic gradient.** Malay and Indian residents carry markedly higher
obesity and diabetes than Chinese residents [@zhang2024bmiSg]. The drivers are genetic,
socio-economic, dietary and environmental, not moral, and the gradient motivates culturally tailored
counselling and the national War on Diabetes [@mohWarOnDiabetes]. (The diabetes detail is in the
*Type 2 Diabetes* chapter.)

**National policy gives clinicians tools to point patients toward.** The tools include My Healthy
Plate, Nutri-Grade (whose national roll-out measurably cut the sugar in drinks bought)
[@moh2023nutrigradeimpact; @shin2023nutrigrade] and the Healthier Choice Symbol on packaged foods
[@hpbHealthierChoiceSymbol]. Healthier SG, the enrolled-family-doctor scheme, turns "recognise and
refer" into a longitudinal health plan [@mohHealthierSG].

The 2016 obesity guideline's Asian BMI cut-offs remain current, but its treatment sections predate
the GLP-1 era, so its management content is dated [@hpbmoh2016obesityCPG; @lee2023obesitylandscape].

## Is obesity just "eating too much"? {#sec-close}

The belief comes from the arithmetic of energy balance: weight is gained only when intake exceeds
expenditure, so obesity looks like a matter of eating less. The arithmetic is right, but it leaves out
three things. What is eaten shapes how much is eaten, because ultra-processed foods and
sugar-sweetened drinks push intake past need. Once the surplus is stored, leptin resistance weakens
satiety and the body defends the higher weight. And the harm depends on where the fat sits: visceral
and ectopic fat drive the insulin resistance behind the metabolic-syndrome cluster. Singaporean
adults carry more visceral fat at a given BMI, which is why Singapore reads BMI at lower cut-offs and
always alongside the waist.

Care therefore works on those causes, and the way it is delivered matters too: because weight stigma
can itself promote weight gain, weight-inclusive, person-first care is part of the treatment.
